paper_title: PhysEvolve: Verifier-grounded Self-evolution for Physical Reasoning with Executable Worlds

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Physical reasoning underpins how embodied systems understand and act in the physical world, yet vision-language models (VLMs) remain unreliable on questions about dynamics and physical causality. Progress is critically constrained by the scarcity of grounded counterfactual training data, as observational videos capture only the factual trajectory that occurred. The self-evolving paradigm offers a route beyond fixed datasets by enabling models to construct their own training problems. Extending this paradigm to physics, however, requires an external source of truth that can both validate model-proposed environments and verify alternative physical outcomes under intervention. We introduce \physevolve{}, a verifier-grounded self-evolving framework that trains VLMs for causal physical reasoning from model-proposed executable worlds and simulation-authored tasks. At each round, a shared VLM proposes executable world programs and evidence schemas; a deterministic physics engine freezes each valid world, simulates matched baseline and body-elided counterfactual branches, and synthesizes discrete, answer-bound visual tasks. Exact verifier feedback from task solving updates both the shared policy via GRPO and an adaptive curriculum over physical intents. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, \physevolve{} achieves targeted gains across PhysBench, CausalPhys, and ContPhy without human intervention data, improving PhysBench Throwing by $8.8$ points and ContPhy Counterfactual Removal and Goal-Pit by $7.4$ and $24.4$ points. These gains concentrate on interaction-sensitive and altered-world questions, demonstrating zero-shot transfer of causal principles to unseen complex dynamics (cloth, fluid, soft bodies) and real-world video.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Multimodal understanding of the physical world is foundational to embodied intelligence and robotic systems, where reliable decision-making requires anticipating how scenes evolve and respond to external interventions (Black et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2026). Yet current vision-language models (VLMs) remain substantially less reliable on physical dynamics, intervention effects, and counterfactual outcomes than on static object recognition or spatial relations (Chow et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2024), and broader multimodal reasoning benchmarks echo the same reliability gap on structured logical inputs (Yuan et al., 2026). Closing this gap is fundamentally bottlenecked by training data: high-quality, verifiably annotated examples that isolate how physical outcomes change under controlled interventions are exceptionally scarce. Real-world videos are not only costly to annotate, but fundamentally capture only the factual trajectory that occurred, rendering counterfactual alternatives unobservable (Pearl, 2009). growing paradigm of self-evolving systems circumvents static data bottlenecks by enabling models to autonomously generate the problems from which they learn (Zhao et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026). The viability of this paradigm hinges on an external source of truth that can independently validate self-generated problems and verify their correct answers as the training Equal contribution. Corresponding author: xyyue@ie.cuhk.edu.hk. 1 Preprint. distribution shifts. In symbolic domains such as mathematics and code, an interpreter provides this exact supervision: Proposer generates an executable specification, the interpreter computes its deterministic output, and exact correctness supplies the Solvers learning signal. Physics simulators offer natural counterpart for the physical world by executing proposed environments and exposing their complete internal states (Prabhudesai et al., 2026). This analogy suggests an appealingly direct route to physical self-play: retain the proposersolver curriculum and substitute physics simulator for the symbolic interpreter. However, naively mapping this paradigm to physical reasoning reveals fundamental structural breakdown (Figure 1). When shared ProposerSolver policy proposes rigid-body scenes and evaluates single simulated trajectory using continuous proximity scores, two failure modes emerge (Section 3.1): (1) single-trajectory readouts cannot construct or verify intervention tasks, starving the curriculum of causal supervision; and (2) continuous proximity rewards inflate learnability signals for uniformly incorrect rollouts, inducing reward hacking without improving exact physical correctness. These findings establish two indispensable requirements for physical self-play: the verification environment must actively execute interventions across paired branches, and derived visual tasks must be bound to discrete, exact ground truth. We introduce PhysEvolve, verifier-grounded self-evolving framework that learns causal physical reasoning from policy-proposed executable worlds and simulation-authored tasks (Figure 2). Rather than authoring text questions directly, task-conditioned Proposer generates an executable world program and an evidence schema. deterministic physics executor validates and freezes the scene, executes matched baseline and body-elided counterfactual branches under identical initial conditions, and derives an answer-bound question from their divergent outcomes. The shared VLM then solves the task from the baseline video, receiving exact discrete feedback. This architecture establishes strict information boundary: the policy guides the exploration of physical environments, while the fixed simulator alone determines physical validity and factual/counterfactual ground truth. The resulting exact solver feedback simultaneously drives shared-policy updates via GRPO and guides an adaptive curriculum over physical reasoning intents. Training on executor-synthesized tasks over policy-proposed worlds produces targeted transfer across three physical-reasoning benchmarks without any human-annotated intervention data. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025a), PhysEvolve improves PhysBench Throwing by 8.78 percentage points and Judgment by 5.08 points. Crucially, on ContPhy, performance on Counterfactual Removal and Goal-Pit increases by 7.38 and 24.44 points, transferring causal intervention principles zero-shot to held-out continuous media (cloth, fluid, rope, and soft bodies) entirely absent from the rigid-body training templates. On real-world videos in CausalPhys, PhysEvolve likewise achieves consistent gains on Anticipation (+2.46) and Intervention (+2.27). Our core contributions are summarized as follows: 1. Verifier-grounded physical self-play: We present PhysEvolve, the first self-evolving framework that trains VLMs for causal physical reasoning via model-proposed executable worlds, enforcing strict information boundary between policy exploration and deterministic simulator verification. 2. Intervention-grounded task synthesis: We introduce an execution pipeline that executes matched baseline and body-elided branches under identical seeds, transforming continuous multi-body dynamics into discrete, answer-bound multi-choice tasks with exact verifier rewards. 3. Out-of-distribution causal transfer & audit: We demonstrate that self-play on rigid-body programs transfers zero-shot to complex continuous dynamics and real-world video, and provide an empirical audit exposing why naive single-trajectory physical self-play fundamentally collapses.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Physical reasoning in vision-language models. Extensive studies reveal that current multimodal models handle static visual appearance and geometric arrangements far more reliably than temporal prediction, physical intervention, and counterfactual reasoning (Riochet et al., 2018; Bear et al., 2021; Tung et al., 2023; Yi et al., 2020; Ates et al., 2022; Chow et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026). Broader multimodal reasoning benchmarks further expose that vision-language models remain unreliable on structured logical reasoning (Yuan et al., 2026), motivating verifiable, grounded 2 Preprint. supervision rather than perception-only training. To diagnose physical understanding beyond passive prediction, counterfactual benchmarks introduce paired simulator-generated alternative trajectories and intervention questions (Baradel et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022; Patel et al., 2022). Recently, simulator-grounded training has emerged to convert simulation traces into verifiable supervision: notably, Sim2Reason synthesizes physics QA pairs from predefined simulator rollouts and filters shortcut solutions (Prabhudesai et al., 2026). Unlike offline trajectory-to-QA pipelines, PhysEvolve autonomously synthesizes verifiable counterfactual supervision online by executing paired intervention branches over active, policy-proposed physical worlds. Self-evolving agents and environment co-design. While standard self-training bootstraps reasoning over fixed problem sets (Zelikman et al., 2022; Gulcehre et al., 2023), self-evolving agents generate the very curricula and environments from which they learn. Absolute Zero pioneered shared-policy proposersolver self-play with code interpreters (Zhao et al., 2025), inspiring subsequent frameworks to expand task substrates across multi-agent debates, geometric spaces, games, and tool-augmented execution (Huang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). complementary line of modular and agentic multimodal systemsspanning visual-to-code generation, agentic coding for games, search-augmented image generation, multimodal deep search, agentic perception, and failure-aware software repairdemonstrates that decomposing perception, planning, and execution into verifiable sub-routines scales reliably across complex tool-use environments (Jiang et al., 2026b;a; Feng et al., 2026a; Jiao et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2026). In parallel, unsupervised environment design (UED) co-evolves adaptive environments alongside control policies based on learner regret or progress (Wang et al., 2019; Dennis et al., 2020; Parker-Holder et al., 2022; Zala et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2024). While existing self-play frameworks operate primarily in discrete symbolic spaces, PhysEvolve shifts the frontier of self-evolution to continuous multi-body physics, delegating the physical environment proposal to the policy while retaining deterministic verification and task synthesis within the executor. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) substitutes brittle, exploitable learned reward models with deterministic, ground-truth verifiers in domains admitting objective computation (DeepSeek-AI, 2025; Lambert et al., 2024). Verification methods have expanded from exact answer matching and test-suite execution to hybrid dense-sparse rewards, self-consistency checks, and formal proof checking (Tao et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026; Wilf et al., 2026). Recent multimodal RL work further studies reward design under heterogeneous or competing objectives, including multi-task visual reasoning with moving-average reward normalization, thinking-with-image video reward models, and reasoning reward models for agents (Feng et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2026). While RLVR has achieved remarkable success in mathematical deduction and program synthesis, extending objective verification to multimodal physical reasoning has remained an open challenge. PhysEvolve realizes RLVR for multimodal physics by grounding policy updates in discrete, simulation-verified causal outcomes rather than heuristic continuous proximity metrics.

sections.title: 3 METHODOLOGY
sections.content: We introduce PhysEvolve, verifier-grounded self-evolving framework that learns causal physical reasoning by having shared visionlanguage policy propose executable worlds while deterministic physics executor authors and verifies derived multimodal tasks. Below, Section 3.1 first diagnoses the structural pitfalls of naively transferring code self-play to physical reasoning and establishes two necessary design principles. Sections 3.23.5 then detail the framework architecture, the task-conditioned proposer, the intervention-grounded task synthesis pipeline, and the hierarchical co-evolution training loop.

sections.title: 3.1 PROBLEM FORMULATION AND PITFALLS OF NAIVE PHYSICAL SELF-PLAY
sections.content: In discrete symbolic domains such as mathematics and code synthesis, self-play enables models to surpass fixed data limits by autonomously generating and solving their own problems (Zhao et al., 2025). The policy evolves by optimizing learnability reward that dynamically prioritizes tasks near the boundary of its current competence. The viability of this paradigm stems from its objectivity: 3 Preprint. Figure 1: Naive self-play baseline for physical reasoning. Proposer generates world program; the executor simulates single trajectory and derives Forward, Inverse, and Parameter tasks. Graded continuous proximity can reward Solver that remains fundamentally incorrect, broadcasting distorted learnability signals back to the Proposer. deterministic interpreter executes model-written specifications and returns exact correctness signals without human supervision. Given that grounded, intervention-level annotations are exceptionally scarce in physical reasoning, transferring this self-play paradigm to multimodal physics by substituting physics simulator for the symbolic interpreter appears to be natural solution. In direct physical transfer, shared ProposerSolver policy interacts with rigid-body simulator. For each proposed world W, the executor simulates one factual trajectory τ under seed ξ, extracts an observation alongside simulator-derived target y, and scores the Solvers prediction ˆy via graded similarity metric s: τ = Φξ(W), (x, y) = readout(τ ), rnaive = s(ˆy, y). (1) Here Φξ denotes deterministic simulation and assigns partial credit based on continuous numerical or spatial proximity, intended to prevent sparse, uninformative all-zero rewards early in training. While this transfer ostensibly preserves both autonomous task generation and verifiable supervision, empirical auditing reveals two fatal structural failure modes. Failure Mode 1: Single-trajectory execution cannot ground causal interventions. Physical reasoning distinctively demands understanding how scenes respond to counterfactual interventions outcomes that never occurred in the observed trajectory (Pearl, 2009). However, evaluating single trajectory τ restricts the task space strictly to passive observational readouts (e.g., predicting an objects future position or initial velocity). In our audit of the naive transfer baseline, exactly zero intervention or counterfactual tasks were synthesized across 100 training rounds, causing PhysBench dynamics accuracy to stagnate and reasoning performance to degrade (Section 4.4). This limitation is structural: causal ground truth cannot be inferred from single trajectory without paired, counterfactual branch executions. Neither scaling model capacity nor expanding rollout volume can produce verified labels that lie beyond the verification interface itself. Failure Mode 2: Graded proximity rewards induce learnability illusions. In code and math, execution verification yields rigorous binary correctness signal. In continuous physics, however, substituting exact match with graded proximity fundamentally distorts reinforcement signals. Because scores relative closeness rather than true task resolution, clusters of uniformly incorrect rollouts (e.g., predicting stationary velocities or median parameters) yield intermediate rewards. These reward distributions artificially inflate the empirical learnability metric rlearn = 1 2a 0.5, misleading the curriculum into classifying failed, trivial tasks as productive learning boundaries. Consequently, graded reward steadily increases during naive training while exact physical correctness remains near zero (Section 4.4, Table 4). These failure modes establish that continuous physics cannot be treated as trivial drop-in replacement for discrete code interpreters. Autonomous physical reasoning requires two non-negotiable architectural guarantees: 1. Branch-level verification: The executor must actively execute paired, counterfactual interventions (divergent simulation branches) under identical initial conditions to establish objective causal ground truth. 2. Discrete answer binding: Derived physical tasks must map continuous trajectories into discrete, answer-bound problems, ensuring that Solver success reflects exact correctness rather than deceptive proximity. 4 Preprint. sections.title: 3.2 FRAMEWORK OVERVIEW
sections.content: Guided by these requirements, we introduce PhysEvolve (Figure 2). At each round, TaskConditioned Proposer transforms sampled reasoning intent into an executable candidate world. Through Intervention-Grounded Task Synthesis, fixed executor establishes factual and counterfactual outcomes via deterministic simulation and synthesizes discrete, answer-bound multiple-choice questions. Finally, Co-Evolution Training translates exact Solver correctness into joint updates for the shared policy and an adaptive curriculum. Let πθ denote the shared visionlanguage policy. The identical parameters serve as Proposer πP θ and Solver πS θ . The Proposer controls the exploration of executable physical environments, while the Solver receives only rendered baseline video observations and the resulting question and options. Crucially, strict information boundary is enforced: the fixed physics executor alone accesses internal simulator states, computes counterfactual branches, and binds the correct answer. This boundary enables the policy to actively shape its own training distribution without ever setting its own training labels, eliminating label contamination and reward hacking.

sections.title: 3.3 TASK-CONDITIONED PROPOSER
sections.content: The Proposer receives reasoning intent σ, which specifies the target physical relation to probe and the evidence required to make that relation uniquely decidable. Grounded in classical cognitive physics (Battaglia et al., 2013; Spelke, 1990), we instantiate simulation across three fundamental Newtonian paradigms: (1) projectile motion and parabolic dynamics (Throwing), (2) impulsemomentum transfer and kinematic collisions (Collision), and (3) continuous kinematics and contact interactions (Motion), spanning eight active reasoning intents. Conditioned on σ, the Proposer samples tuple (W, S) πP θ ( σ): an executable world program and an evidence schema S. The world program is authored in PhysDSL (a domain-specific Python API over rigid-body simulation) specifying 3D geometry, material properties (mass, restitution, friction), initial states, kinematic constraints, and rendering viewpoints. The evidence schema declares the semantic roles of key entities (e.g., query projectiles, barrier obstacles, potential collision targets) required by intent σ. The executor validates these role declarations against the realized simulation, rejecting any proposal whose physical dynamics cannot support the requested reasoning intent. Complete specifications of PhysDSL and evidence schemas are provided in Appendices and A.2. 5 Preprint. 3.4 INTERVENTION-GROUNDED TASK SYNTHESIS candidate pair (W, S) represents only potential reasoning opportunity; simulation execution must establish its physical semantics before it can constitute valid training task. The executor admits an item only when execution recovers unambiguous physical evidence that determines unique answer. This contract is executed across three sequential stages: World verification and freezing. The executor parses and executes the world program in sandboxed simulator, resolving evidence-schema roles against simulated rigid bodies. It admits only worlds exhibiting valid geometry, non-trivial physical events, and the causal prerequisites of intent σ. bounded deterministic repair stage corrects minor placement or boundary syntax violations without introducing new bodies or joints. Once admitted, the world definition is strictly frozen into an immutable scene definition. Freezing guarantees that all subsequent intervention branches share identical initial geometry, material properties, and simulation seeds, ensuring that divergent outcomes are strictly attributable to declared interventions. Branch elision. For interventional reasoning intents, the executor constructs finite set of body removals Bσ. For each Bσ, it elides those bodies and their dependent constraints from the frozen world, yielding the matched execution pair: (cid:0)τ, τB (cid:1) = (cid:0)Φξ(W), Φξ(W B)(cid:1), Bσ. (2) Both trajectories share the identical simulator state, random seed ξ, and time horizon. The Solver observes only video rendering of the factual trajectory τ, while the executor retains the divergent branch trajectories {τB} as objective ground truth. Answer-bound question synthesis. Each reasoning intent defines discrete readout function, feasibility margins, and natural language templates. The executor applies the readout across baseline and branch trajectories. An item is suppressed if readouts are non-unique, infeasible, or fall within sensitive physical margin thresholds (e.g., velocity differences below 0.30 m/s). Otherwise, the executor determines the unique factual or counterfactual outcome, binds it to ground-truth option index {A, B, C, D}, and renders the final visual question and distractors. For inverse intervention tasks (e.g., Which wall should be removed to make the ball land in the target pit?), the executor runs all candidate elisions (remove A, remove B, remove both) and validates whether exactly one branch achieves the goal; none of the above is selected only if no branch reaches the target. Detailed contracts, margin tests, and binding rules are documented in Appendix C.

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Research questions. We design our empirical evaluation around four central questions: (Q1) Targeted capability transfer: Does PhysEvolve yield targeted improvements on the specific physical capabilities it simulates during training? (Q2) Out-of-distribution transfer: Do causal principles learned in synthetic rigid-body environments generalize to unseen complex media (fluid, cloth, soft bodies) and real-world video? (Q3) Architectural necessity: How critically do paired branch simulation and joint ProposerSolver optimization contribute to performance? (Q4) Failure anatomy: What exact supervisory signals are forfeited by relying on single-trajectory execution and continuous proximity rewards? Training configuration. All experimental variants are initialized from the open-weight base model Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025a). Training is executed in single run for 100 steps using one-epoch GRPO with learning rate of 106. At each step, the curriculum samples = 4 reasoning intents and generates = 4 world program proposals per intent, capping retention at 32 active Solver groups with 4 rollouts per group. The complete hyperparameters and training loop are detailed in Appendix and Algorithm 2. Benchmarks and evaluation protocols. We evaluate across three rigorous physical reasoning benchmarks: (1) PhysBench (Chow et al., 2025) covers broad static and dynamic physical QA over 9,802 items; (2) ContPhy (Zheng et al., 2024) benchmarks counterfactual and goal-directed physical reasoning across 1,950 scenarios involving complex continuous dynamics (cloth, fluid, rope, and soft bodies); and (3) CausalPhys (Tang et al., 2026) assesses physical anticipation and intervention in 3,057 real-world video scenarios. All evaluated models share identical prompts, visual frame sampling, greedy decoding, and official evaluation protocols (Appendix F.3). Baselines and comparative context. Our primary, strictly matched comparison comprises: (1) the base Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct model; (2) Naive self-play, which replicates single-trajectory execution with continuous graded proximity rewards; and (3) PhysEvolve. To contextualize performance across model scales, we also report unaligned results for prominent open-weight models: InternVL2.5-8B (Chen et al., 2024), Llama-3.2-11B-Vision (Meta, 2024), Pixtral-12B (Agrawal et al., 2024), Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Bai et al., 2025b), and the scaled Qwen3-VL-32B (Bai et al., 2025a).

sections.title: 4.3 ABLATION STUDIES
sections.content: Q3: Necessity of branch-enabled synthesis and joint co-evolution. We investigate the architectural components of PhysEvolve via two targeted endpoint ablations: Essentiality of paired branch execution. In Table 2, removing branch simulation and its dependent Counterfactual/Inverse task families sharply degrades downstream causal transfer. The performance drop is especially drastic on ContPhy Counterfactual Removal (8.20 points) and Goal-Pit (23.33 points), dropping performance back to the un-finetuned Base level. This ablation empirically confirms that paired branch elision is the indispensable engine for acquiring causal physical reasoning. Criticality of joint ProposerSolver optimization. In Table 3, we freeze Proposer role updates, training the shared policy exclusively via Solver rollouts. Without co-evolution, the policy undergoes severe representational collapse: accuracy drops precipitously to 15.01% on CausalPhys and 17.85% on ContPhy, accompanied by collapse in answer parse rate (falling to 26.07% on CausalPhys and 0% in later steps). Updating the Proposer keeps world generation diverse and physically non-trivial, preventing the Solver from over-adapting to degenerate data stream.

sections.title: 4.4 AUDITING THE SINGLE-TRAJECTORY INTERFACE
sections.content: Q4: What causes naive physical self-play to collapse? We conduct an empirical audit of the single-trajectory verifier and task stream in Naive self-play to validate the theoretical pitfalls identified in Section 3.1. Divergence between graded reward and exact correctness. Table 4 exposes striking pathology: continuous proximity rewards consistently provide deceptive reinforcement. For Forward prediction, rollouts achieve high mean graded reward of 0.373 despite zero exact matches across all 100 rounds. For Inverse and Parameter tasks, mean rewards reach 0.664 and 0.787 while exact accuracy remains below 7%. An error audit reveals severe mode collapse: the policy learns to output sta9 Preprint. tionary initial velocities (746 instances) or the median rung of the parameter ladder (145 instances), exploiting the graded metric to reap partial credit without solving the physical events. Task space starvation. Over 100 training rounds, the naive single-trajectory verifier generated zero intervention questions and zero counterfactual tasks. Constrained to an un-intervened factual trajectory τ , the system is incapable of synthesizing causal supervision. Consequently, downstream PhysBench dynamics accuracy stagnates  (Table 1)  .

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: PhysEvolve demonstrates that verifier-grounded self-evolution extends to continuous multimodal physical reasoning by anchoring self-play in executable 3D world programs and paired counterfactual branches. Converting continuous physics into discrete verifier contracts eliminates the dual traps of continuous reward hacking and causal blindness inherent in naive physical self-play. Strong targeted gains on Newtonian dynamics and zero-shot transfer to unseen continuous media and real-world video show that counterfactual execution provides scalable foundation for generalizable physical intelligence in vision-language models, entirely without any human-annotated physical reasoning supervision during self-play training. Each training target is bound to verified physical outcome.
